interactions: Tamoxifen: no pharmacokinetic interaction expected (tamoxifen is metabolised mainly by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4); tamoxifen can also raise transaminases, so share the scheduled liver tests with oncology.
Sertraline: no clinically significant interaction with riluzole expected.
Ferrous sulfate: no clinically significant interaction expected.
output.summary: No interaction requires a change to riluzole 50 mg twice daily; tamoxifen can also raise transaminases, so share the liver tests with oncology. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for the first 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x ULN. Report any febrile illness (check the white cell count for neutropenia).
warnings: Hepatotoxicity: measure ALT and AST before the first dose, monthly for the first 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x ULN.
Neutropenia (rare): the patient should report any febrile illness, and the white cell count should then be checked.
Existing regimen: sertraline is a moderate CYP2D6 inhibitor and can lower endoxifen, the active metabolite of tamoxifen; flag to oncology.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Active denervation with chronic neurogenic change in cervical and lumbosacral limb muscles, fibrillation potentials in cervical and thoracic paraspinals, and tongue fasciculation potentials; reduced CMAPs with normal conduction velocities and no conduction block; normal sensory studies.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No intracranial metastasis and no leptomeningeal or dural enhancement after gadolinium; nonspecific corticospinal tract and motor cortex signal change is supportive only.
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs; including metastasis or leptomeningeal disease after breast cancer; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No cord compression, epidural disease, vertebral metastasis, intramedullary lesion or leptomeningeal enhancement after gadolinium; normal cord signal.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 542 U/L (3.2x ULN); paraneoplastic antibodies negative; blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, ESR and CRP normal.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP; plus a paraneoplastic antibody panel
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic: a paraneoplastic antibody panel because of the breast cancer history.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Acellular CSF with mildly raised protein (48 mg/dL), normal glucose, negative cytology and no clonal population on flow cytometry.
action_criteria.label: CSF with cytology and flow cytometry, only because the breast cancer history raises a leptomeningeal or paraneoplastic question
action_criteria.rationale: CSF is not part of the routine ALS work-up. Here the breast cancer history raises a leptomeningeal or paraneoplastic question; CSF does not diagnose ALS.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 84% predicted, SNIP 76 cmH2O and NIF -78 cmH2O are within normal limits: baseline for 3-monthly monitoring.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic variant on the ALS gene panel; a negative result does not exclude a genetic contribution.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. It is offered with counselling to people with ALS because a pathogenic variant changes counselling for relatives and may open gene-targeted treatment or trials.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pharmacokinetic interaction with tamoxifen, sertraline or ferrous sulfate; tamoxifen can also raise transaminases, so liver tests are shared with oncology; the existing sertraline and tamoxifen (CYP2D6, endoxifen) point is flagged to oncology.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established
action_criteria.rationale: Riluzole is metabolised by CYP1A2 and can raise liver transaminases, so the medicine list, alcohol use and baseline liver function are reviewed before treatment. Tamoxifen can also raise transaminases, so liver test results are shared with oncology.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat ALS with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange: they have no benefit.
Do not stop respiratory monitoring because the baseline values are normal.
Do not attribute the progressive weakness, wasting or bulbar signs to anxiety or a functional disorder.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive bilateral hand weakness spreading to the legs with upper motor neuron signs (brisk jaw jerk, limb hyperreflexia, bilateral Hoffman signs, a right Babinski sign and a spastic gait) and lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar (tongue atrophy and fasciculations), cervical and lumbosacral regions on examination and EMG, with active denervation also in thoracic paraspinal muscles, with mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests; disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with the patient and family.

Repeat FVC and SNIP about every 3 months and ask at each review about orthopnoea, morning headache, daytime sleepiness and unrefreshing sleep, referring for NIV assessment when these appear or values fall.
Arrange a speech and language therapy assessment of speech and swallowing, with communication support, and monitor weight and swallowing at each review.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.
Inform her oncology team of the diagnosis and coordinate the riluzole liver test monitoring with them; tamoxifen continues unchanged.

Refer to a specialist ALS multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), reviewed about every 2 to 3 months, with an early, patient-paced discussion of advance care planning.
Offer genetic counselling and, if the patient wishes, ALS genetic testing, explaining the implications for relatives.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: brisk jaw jerk, limb hyperreflexia, bilateral Hoffman signs, a right Babinski sign and a spastic gait with lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar (tongue atrophy and fasciculations), cervical and lumbosacral regions, with active denervation also in thoracic paraspinal muscles (limb-onset ALS phenotype).
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.
Normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block argue against multifocal motor neuropathy, and normal sensory responses argue against a sensorimotor neuropathy.
CK 542 U/L (3.2x ULN): mild to moderate elevation is common in ALS from denervation and does not by itself suggest a myopathy.

FVC 84% predicted and SNIP 76 cmH2O are normal at baseline. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).

After treated breast cancer, gadolinium MRI of the brain and spine, CSF cytology with flow cytometry and paraneoplastic antibodies answer the leptomeningeal and paraneoplastic question; all are negative here, and paraneoplastic motor neuron disease is rare.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The cancer is in remission; gadolinium MRI shows no metastatic or leptomeningeal disease, CSF cytology and flow cytometry are negative, paraneoplastic antibodies are negative, and the upper motor neuron signs with multi-region denervation show a primary motor neuron disorder.

findings.finding: Bilateral FDI: fibrillations +2, positive sharp waves +2, complex fasciculation potentials, large amplitude long duration polyphasic MUPs, severely reduced recruitment. Cervical paraspinals C6-C8: fibrillations +1 bilaterally.
Bilateral tibialis anterior: fibrillations +1, fasciculation potentials, mildly large MUPs, reduced recruitment. Right gastrocnemius: fasciculation potentials.
T6-T8 bilateral paraspinals: fibrillations +1, sparse fasciculations.
Tongue: fasciculation potentials without clear fibrillations on this examination.
All sensory studies normal: median, ulnar, sural and superficial peroneal SNAPs within normal limits bilaterally.

specialized_test.impression: 1. Active denervation (fibrillation potentials, positive sharp waves) and chronic reinnervation (large, long-duration, polyphasic MUPs with severely reduced recruitment) in cervical and lumbosacral limb muscles, with fibrillation potentials in the cervical (C6-C8) and thoracic (T6-T8) paraspinal muscles. 2. Fasciculation potentials in the tongue without fibrillation potentials on this study. 3. Reduced median and ulnar CMAP amplitudes with normal conduction velocities; no conduction block. 4. Normal sensory nerve conduction studies. The findings indicate a widespread disorder of anterior horn cells.

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. C is a 55-year-old right-handed woman with a history of stage I breast cancer treated 4 years ago, presenting with a 10-month history of progressive bilateral hand weakness and muscle twitching. She first noticed difficulty typing and clicking a computer mouse approximately 10 months ago, initially thinking this was repetitive strain injury or carpal tunnel syndrome related to her demanding desk job.

Over the following months, the weakness clearly progressed beyond what would be expected for entrapment neuropathy. She noticed wasting of the muscles between her fingers and at the base of her thumbs. She has developed frequent cramps in her hands and forearms, particularly at night. Her family has noticed muscle twitching in her forearms and calves, which she describes as spontaneous and not triggered by activity.

Approximately 4-5 months ago, she developed mild bilateral ankle dorsiflexor weakness, noticing her feet beginning to scuff the floor. She denies any sensory symptoms, bladder changes, or swallowing difficulties. She has no back or neck pain.

Her most recent oncology review, including CT chest and breast examination, showed no recurrence. Given her breast cancer history, her oncologist was concerned about a paraneoplastic syndrome or leptomeningeal metastasis and referred her urgently to neurology.
